reasons: The four Vedic anchors do pair dyaúḥ/pitā́ with pr̥thivī́/mātā́ as claimed, but that is one tradition. The only non-Indic anchor, Hes. Th. 284, has χθόνα with μητέρα as 'mother of flocks' (μήλων), an epithet, not a Sky-father/Earth-mother pairing. Outside Indic the earth word is renewed everywhere, so the inherited content comes down to 'mother' (and 'father') applied to earth and sky, and Earth-as-mother is near-universal. Pind. O. 7.38 (Οὐρανός beside Γαῖα + μάτηρ) is a good Greek comparandum. The Lucretian support (1.250, 2.992: Pater, Mater, terra) is a philosophical commonplace, probably Greek-derived (Aither/Gaia), not independent Italic evidence. Defensible, not compelling.

Ved. ūrdhvá- = Gk ὀρθός and *steh2- are sound, but 'stand upright' is a compositional phrase that any language forms from its words for 'upright' and 'stand'. AVŚ 9.9.19 is the AV recension of RV 1.164.10b, not independent. The contexts do not match: a cosmogonic riddle, an assembly standing for fear of Achilles, Cato's iron post that must stand vertical. Latin rectus is not cognate. Nothing beyond chance co-occurrence of two frequent inherited words.

The anchors themselves are split. AVŚ 12.2.29 has vīreṣu but itemises the livestock (aśveṣu, goṣu, aja, aviṣu). Cato 141.3 has pecua but pastores for 'men'. The cited support, though, carries the exact two-member cognate dyad in congruent protective prayers: Umbr. ueiro + pequo with salua + seritu (Iguvine VIa 30, 32, verified in Buck); Av. pasu + vīra (Y 9.4, Yt 5.3); Av. θrāθrāi with pasuuā̊ + vīraiiā̊, 'for the protection of cattle and men' (Yt 13); AVP 19.56 paśubhiś + vīraiḥ. Cato's Mars prayer (salua + seruassis) matches the Umbrian verb phrase. Same genre (apotropaic prayer for a community's men and herds), a specific binomial, not a chance pairing. Accepted on the formula; the AV anchor is only a loose instance.

Ved. āśú- = Gk ὠκύς and áśva- = ἵππος (*h1éḱwos) are exact. The full pair is in the Vedic support (āśúm + áśvam RV 7.71.5b, 10.107.10a; áśvāḥ + āśávaḥ drawing a chariot, RV 10.119.3b) and matches the Homeric formulaic ὠκέας + ἵππους, here in yoking contexts with ζυγόν (*yewg-) beside Ved. yuktā́saḥ. The anchor RV 1.118.4b has āśávaḥ with pataṃgā́ḥ (birds), a renewal, but the support carries the pair. 'Swift horses' carries some generic risk, but the exact adjective as a stock team epithet in both branches makes this a sound inherited formula.

Gk κύκλος + ἀελίοιο (Eur. El. 465, the sun on Achilles' shield) and Vedic cakrám + sū́ryasya (RV 4.17.14, 5.29.10; sū́raḥ + cakrám 1.130.9; all support) are an exact two-member cognate pair, and ON fagrahvél is a name for the sun: a defensible case. Against it: Greek κύκλος here means 'disc'; a sun seen as circle or wheel is visually natural; the Greek is late (tragedy); Lucretius' rota is a different word and plausibly modelled on Greek; and the AV anchors (13.2.11, 13.2.15) are about the sun's chariot and team, a different image. The Vedic myth (Indra tearing off the sun's wheel) is unlike the Greek description. Weak.

The root *gʷʰen- is shared (Ved. hantár-, Gk φονεύς/φονεύω, ON bani, OE bana), but each is the ordinary word for 'kill/killer' in its language, the suffixes are independent, and an agent noun with an objective genitive is generic syntax. The objects differ (śátrūṇām, asurāṇām, dasyūnām vs Σφιγγός, μητρός). The Germanic anchor is misplaced: Grímnismál 54 is the prose end-link, where bana means 'death' ('got his death'), not an epithet. Real bani/bonan + genitive cases (Hundings, Ongenþēowes) are only in support. Phoen. 1507 has an aorist participle (φονεύσας), not an agent noun. Inheritance is shown only at root level; no specific dragon-slaying collocation here.

'Burning/kindled fire' is a generic phrase built on the basic verb of burning. The nouns differ between Greek (πυρός) and Vedic (agní-). Latin aestifer is a Lucretian compound adjective from aestus, not a participle; its partner ignis is the only point of contact with Vedic. Vedic samidhāná/sámiddha is ritual kindling, Greek αἰθομένοιο descriptive in similes, Lucretius physics: the contexts are not comparable. Coincidence of frequent words.

The anchors do not carry the claimed collocation. Il. 23.183 and PV 370 use δάπτω (not *h1ed-), and Beo. 3144 has fire (fȳra) but no 'eat' verb. The *h1ed- verb is only in support: Il. 23.182 ἐσθίει; Beo. 3015, 3115 fretan, whose subjects brond and glēd are not cognate with πῦρ. 'Fire devours' is typologically common (Semitic etc.), and *h1ed- is the basic 'eat' verb in each language, so the co-occurrence is expected. The cremation setting is shared but follows from the subject matter.

The same image as C005, with weaker anchors. Lat. rota and Ved. rátha- are cognate, but equating Lucretius' solis + rota ('the sun's disc') with sūryasya + ratham ('the sun's chariot', AVŚ 13.1.47, 13.2.15) treats a lexical shift that predates the texts as phraseological drift. 'The sun drives a chariot' is a different image (cf. Greek Helios). AVŚ 9.9.3 = the RV 1.164 riddle and does not name the sun. The only real support is again Vedic cakrám + sū́ryasya vs Gk κύκλος + ἡλίου, and Lucretius is likely Hellenizing. Weak.

Ved. dám-pati- = Gk δεσ-πότης (*dems pótis) is a certain inherited compound, but it is one lexeme, not phraseology: the passages share this word and nothing else. The contexts differ: Vedic dual dampatī is the married couple blessed with prosperity, Hec. 617 δεσπότας the captive women's new masters. True as etymology, only weakly relevant as inherited wording.

*yewg- + *h1éḱwos (Ved. yuj- + áśva-, Gk ζεύγνυμι + ἵππους, Lat. iungo + equos) are exact, but yoking horses is the technical, compositional use of the yoke verb and would arise in any language with these words. Several anchors lack the horse word (RV 9.63.9b, RV 1.161.7d; Od. 6.73 has ἡμιόνους, mules) or use the ζυγόν periphrasis. The Latin anchor is explicitly derivative: Lucr. 5.403 retells Phaethon, and 5.405 cites the old Greek poets (Graium, poetae). The only more specific element, Dawn yoking her team (RV 1.92.15 ~ Od. 23.244-6), is in support.

The *wiHro- / *peḱu dyad is real (see C003), but these anchors are poor instances. AVŚ 16.8.1 has paśavo and vīrā in a long list of what is 'ours', separated by prajā; it is not a dyad. Cato 149.2 is a grazing lease, where herdsmen or livestock being liable for damage is a natural legal pairing; pastores and familia are not cognate, and uiri appears in the unrelated arbitration phrase. AVP 19.56.8 (suvīreṇa with haviṣā) lacks paśu; the paśubhiś + vīraiḥ refrain is in s26-32. Defensible only through support.

*swéh2du- + *médhu with both members cognate in three branches: Ved. svādóḥ + mádhvaḥ (RV 1.84.10), svā́diṣṭham + mádhvaḥ (8.49.4), svādv + madhv (AVP 5.28.8); Gk formulaic μέθυ + ἡδύ; OE swētne + medo (Finn. 39). The contexts are congruent: drink at a feast or offering, the host's gift. A honey-drink is naturally 'sweet', which is some generic risk, but the exact adjective-noun pair recurs as a fixed formula in Homer and in Germanic heroic verse. Hávamál 19 has mjöð but no 'sweet' and adds nothing.

The two anchors share no cognate: OE worda/worca vs Lat. facto/dicto. The cognate links (weorc = ἔργον, word = uerbum) run only through the Greek support, with a different word for 'word' in each branch. 'Word and deed' is a universal merism. Coincidence/generic.

Ved. tr̥p- = Gk τέρπομαι and Ved. pā-/pītí- = Gk πίνω are sound. The best evidence is in support: Hom. τάρπημεν with partitive genitives ἐδητύος, ποτῆτος vs Ved. tr̥pṇuhi + sómasya, both *terp- 'have one's fill' + genitive of food/drink. The anchors are looser: RV 8.82.6c has nouns (pītím, tr̥ptím); Od. 15.391 τέρπεο is the drifted 'enjoy yourself' beside πῖνε; Op. 115 τέρποντ' has no drink element. 'Drink and be sated' is close to generic. Defensible, not compelling.

Gk στεῖραν + βοῦν = Ved. staryàm + gā́m (RV 1.116.22d) is a real exact two-member cognate NP. But it is a lexical pastoral term: the adjective is specialised for female animals, so pairing it with 'cow' is expected. The contexts differ: the Odyssey vows a barren cow as sacrifice to the dead, the RV miracle makes the barren cow swell with milk. The Vedic side is only in support, and the Latin anchor (steriles, of human couples, Lucr. 4.1240) is irrelevant to the NP.

Ved. dr̥śé/dr̥śan + sū́ryam 'to see the sun' = to live (RV 1.23.21c with jyók; 7.104.24d) and Hom. ὁρᾷ + φάος + ἠελίοιο (Il. 18.61) are a real thematic match. But the collocation is split between renewals (Greek renews the verb with ὁράω or the object with φάος), and 'see the sun/light' = 'live' is widespread outside IE (Semitic). Two anchors are misread. In Eur. HF 564, δεδορκότες governs ἀμοιβάς, and φῶς (563) is the object of ἀναβλέψεσθε. The Latvian daina (BV 18879) is literal: no sun or moon (sauli, mēnesi) is visible under the spruces at the in-laws'; it is not a death image.

The underlying *wiHro- *peḱu protection formula is genuine (Umbr. ueiro + pequo with salua + seritu; Av. θrāθrāi with pasuuā̊ + vīraiiā̊). AVŚ 8.7.22 trāyantām with puruṣaṃ + paśum, where trā- = Av. θrā-, is a nice Indo-Iranian match. But the anchors carry only renewals. puruṣa- replaces *wiHro-. AVŚ 11.2.18 is Paśupati's five-animal classification (puruṣa counted as a paśu), not the men-and-cattle dyad. Cato 149.2 is a legal lease (pastores, pecus), not a protection prayer. The *treh2- verb link is internal to Indo-Iranian. Weak as anchored.

The 'see' roots differ (Ved. dr̥ś- < *derḱ-, Lat. uid- < *weyd-). Only the privative prefix is shared, a grammatical morpheme, not a lexical item. 'X and un-X' polar merisms are productive in both languages, and the shared apotropaic context (unseen pests or diseases) follows from the subject. The AV anchor line 6.52.3 itself has neither participle: dr̥ṣṭaḥ and adr̥ṣṭa- are in s2 and s4.

An exact two-member cognate vocative: Ved. dyaùḥ + pítar = Gk Ζεῦ + πάτερ (= Lat. Iuppiter), the sky-god's name + 'father' in the same case and order, opening a prayer or wish (Il. 17.645 asks him to save the Achaeans; Il. 7.179 is the army's prayer at the lot; Theognis 731). Not generic (a specific divine name with a kin term) and not derivative. The Vedic instance is genuine and the Greek formula is frequent.

Ved. tanyatú-/stan- = Lat. tonāre/tonitrus (*(s)tenh2-) and Ved. dyú- as the thunderer (dyóḥ with tanyatóḥ; stanáyan with dyaúḥ) are sound. But no non-Indic anchor has the *dyew- element: Lucr. 6.96 has tonitru with caeli (caelum), and Plautus has tonuit with no god named in the line. Latin Iove + tonante is recalled, not attested in these corpora. Greek uses the root only for the earth groaning (Th. 858 στενάχιζε). 'The sky thunders' is natural. Weak.

Ved. śru- = Gk κλύω (*ḱlew-), with the object Ved. vácas- = Gk ἔπος (*wékʷos, the same neuter s-stem) and a 1sg possessor: Ved. śr̥ṇavat + vácāṃsi + me (RV 1.145.3b, 10.65.13c) and stotúḥ + vácaḥ + śṛṇavat (AVŚ 6.2.1) ~ Gk ἐμόν + ἔπος + ἔκλυες (Il. 14.234 = 16.236). The speech act is the same: the god as hearer of the worshipper's word in prayer. 'Hear my word' has generic risk, but both lexemes are exact, including the specific s-stem rather than an everyday word for 'speech'. RV 7.8.5c and Il. 10.295 have only the verb and are marginal.

A single shared root: Ved. stanayanti (rains thundering from the cloud) vs Gk στενάχουσι (torrents roaring into the sea). The formations differ (-aya- vs the -αχ- enlargement) and the subjects are not cognate. The roar of storm water is a universal image, and στενάχω is a broad verb (Il. 16.393 uses it of horses straight after). Coincidence.

Lat. daps < *dh2p- is fine (de Vaan gives the cognates Gk δάπτω, δαπάνη, ON tafn, Arm. tawn). But the Greek anchors rest on δεῖπνον, which has no accepted etymology (Beekes: 'No etymology; perhaps of Pre-Greek origin'; the link with daps is Furnée's speculation). The one secure Greek cognate in the anchors, δαπάνα in Bacch. 893, means 'expense' in a non-sacrificial sentence. No congruent collocation survives.

The etymology is good: Hitt. kiššari/kišri (loc.) = Gk χειρί (*ǵʰesr-i), Ved. hásta- from the same root; Hitt. dai- = Gk τίθημι = Ved. dhā- (*dʰeh1-). The Hittite loci show keššar + dai- as claimed. But 'put (something) into the hand' is a compositional, near-universal phrase, and 'right hand' cannot be compared lexically (Hittite logogram ZAG vs Ved. dákṣiṇe). The AVP anchor has kṛtaṃ + hastam (a dice formula, 'made in my hand'), not dhā-. Ritual handing-over is broadly comparable. Weak.

Only the verb *bʰer- is shared, and it is the basic verb 'bear/carry' in both languages. The earth nouns differ (bhūmi-/pṛthivī- vs ἄρουρα/γαῖα), and the *dʰéǵʰōm in the reconstructed phrase appears in no passage. 'The earth bears fruit/creatures' is a natural, universal expression. Generic.
